stem: A 39-year-old man who works at an indoor firing range has crampy abdominal pain, irritability and poor memory for several weeks. He now has trouble extending his right wrist. Hemoglobin is low with a small mean cell volume, and his peripheral smear is shown (see the picture).
oneliner: 39M + firing-range worker + colicky abdominal pain + irritability + memory loss + wrist weakness + microcytic anemia → which smear finding?

options.A: Coarse blue dots scattered through small red cells
options.B: Needle-shaped red rods inside myeloid cells
options.C: Neutrophils with six or more nuclear lobes
options.D: Fragmented red cells with pointed edges
options.E: Round purple remnants inside otherwise normal red cells

whyNot.B: **Auer rods** are fused granules in myeloblasts of acute myeloid leukemia, not a lead effect
whyNot.C: **Hypersegmented neutrophils** point to B12 or folate deficiency, which gives a high MCV, not a small one
whyNot.D: **Schistocytes** come from mechanical hemolysis; they do not explain colic and neuropathy
whyNot.E: **Howell-Jolly bodies** are nuclear remnants after splenectomy; they do not explain colic, wrist drop and microcytosis

why: Lead blocks **ALA dehydratase and ferrochelatase** and **pyrimidine 5'-nucleotidase**, so ribosomal RNA is not degraded and clumps as **basophilic stippling**. Colic, wrist drop and microcytosis fit with **lead poisoning**.

idea.rule: Aggregated ribosomal RNA in a red cell appears as blue stippling, and lead is the classic cause.
also: Thalassemia gives basophilic stippling with target cells
Lead lines on the gums and long-bone metaphyses on x-ray
Treatment: succimer or EDTA, with dimercaprol added for encephalopathy
